desc:
Given three strings a, b and c, return the length of the longest string that is a subsequence of all three of them. A subsequence keeps the relative order of the characters it takes but may skip characters.

If the three strings have no common character, return 0.

a = "abcde", b = "ace",  c = "aecd"  ->  2   ("ac" or "ae")
a = "geeks", b = "geeksfor", c = "geeksforgeeks"  ->  5
constraints: All three strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: The two-string LCS looks at one position in each string. What would a state look like with three strings?
Let T(i, j, k) be the answer for the first i characters of a, the first j of b and the first k of c. If all three last characters are equal, T = T(i-1, j-1, k-1) + 1.
Otherwise at least one of the three last characters is not used by the best answer, so take the maximum of T(i-1, j, k), T(i, j-1, k) and T(i, j, k-1). Fill the cube layer by layer over i.
editorial: Extend the pairwise recurrence to three dimensions. T[i][j][k] is the LCS length of the three prefixes. When a[i-1] == b[j-1] == c[k-1] the three characters can be matched together: T[i-1][j-1][k-1] + 1. When they are not all equal, an optimal common subsequence cannot end with all three of them, so one of them is dropped, and the answer is the maximum of the three states obtained by dropping one last character.

The cube has up to 1013, about one million, cells. Layer i depends only on layer i-1 and itself, so two 2-D layers are enough. Note that computing the LCS of two strings and then comparing the result with the third string is not valid: the best pairwise subsequence may be unrelated to the best three-way one.
